bill.liveSenateAfterHouse: The House has already voted on this bill — the Senate decides next. Your senators are the live call.
bill.liveHouseAfterSenate: The Senate has already voted on this bill — the House decides next. Your House member is the live call.
bill.nominationHow: A nomination starts with the President, who picks someone for a government job. From there it belongs to the Senate: a committee reviews the nominee, then the full Senate votes on whether to confirm. The House has no vote on nominations at all.
bill.liveSenateNomination: Only the Senate votes on a nomination — your senators are the live call.
bill.nominationHousePress: Your House member gets no vote here and no formal role — the Senate decides this one alone. What a representative can do is speak up: they share a state with your two senators, and they can press them on a nomination, publicly or privately. So if you call their office, say it plainly — that you know the House has no vote on this, and you're asking your representative to press your state's senators on it. The office logs your call like any other; it just doesn't count toward the Senate's tally.
bill.nominationNoSenator: Only senators vote on a nomination, and your area does not elect any — so there is no senator here for you to call about this one. Your House member has no vote on nominations either; no member of the House does. What their office can still do is speak up, and it logs every call it takes — so if you call, say plainly that you know the House has no vote on this and you want the nomination raised. It just will not count toward the Senate's tally.

This kind of resolution never goes to the President and does not become law.
journey.backTrailerStates: If the {other, select, House {House} Senate {Senate} other {Senate}} changes it, it goes back to the {chamber, select, House {House} Senate {Senate} other {House}} — both chambers have to pass the same text, each by two thirds. A proposed constitutional amendment never goes to the President: it goes to the states, and three quarters of them have to ratify it before it takes effect.

why.title: Why calling works
why.intro: It feels too small to matter. It isn't. Here's what actually happens when you call a congressional office, and why one phone call outweighs a hundred posts.
why.tallyBody: Congressional offices keep a running count of constituent positions on active issues. Those tallies reach the member's desk while a vote is still undecided. Reporting has documented offices overwhelmed by sustained call volume, and members shifting position because of it.
why.emailBody: Congress receives tens of millions of emails a year. Form letters and petition signatures are heavily discounted, and AI-generated mail floods even more so. A phone call is scarce, verifiable effort from a real constituent — that's exactly why it carries more weight.
why.voicemailBody: Offices check voicemail every day and tally messages identically to live calls. If talking to a person isn't for you, after-hours voicemail is a fully effective alternative, not a consolation prize.
why.scriptBody: Your name, your ZIP or town (so they know you're a constituent), the bill, your position, one sentence why. That's it. The whole call takes under a minute, and the staffer is just writing down your position. There's no debate.
why.respectBody: The person answering is usually a young staffer having a long day. Being brief and kind doesn't dilute your message. It makes it land.

privacy.title: Privacy, in plain language
privacy.p1: Oravan has no user accounts. We never ask for your name, email, address, or anything that identifies you.
privacy.p2: Your ZIP code, your issue interests, the bills you have read, and your call history are stored only in your browser's local storage, on your device. When you look up your representatives, the ZIP travels to our server in the page's web address so we can match it to a district — it is used in memory, never stored, and never written to a database. Everything else on this list stays on your device. Your civic record page has a one-tap button that erases all of it.
privacy.p3: When you ask for a call script, your chosen stance and the bill are sent to our server to draft the text, processed in memory, and not linked to any identity. We rate-limit by network address to prevent abuse; we don't keep a log tying addresses to political positions.
privacy.p4: No analytics trackers, no advertising pixels, no cookies at all. Your language preference is kept in your browser's own storage, like everything else personal here.
privacy.p5: This matters because political beliefs are sensitive data. The safest database is the one that doesn't exist, so we didn't build one.
privacy.contact: Questions? Oravan is built in the open — every line of code is inspectable.
privacy.p7: One optional exception to "we never ask": if your ZIP code covers more than one congressional district, you can type your street address to pin down yours. It goes to our server once, is passed straight to the U.S. Census Bureau's public geocoder (so your device never contacts census.gov directly), and is never stored or written to any log. Only the district number comes back.

about.title: About Oravan
about.intro: Oravan is free, nonpartisan civic infrastructure: find your federal representatives, understand active bills in plain language, and make a 30-second call — in English or Spanish, with no account and no server-side record of your political activity.
about.fundingBody: Oravan is independently run and founder-funded. It costs a few hundred dollars a year to host and maintain, currently paid out of one person's pocket. There are no ads, no sponsors, and no investors — and nothing to sell, because we collect no personal data.
about.fundingSupportBody: If Oravan is useful to you, you can chip in to keep it running. Contributions support hosting and upkeep and are not tax-deductible.
about.accountabilityBody: Oravan is an independent, nonpartisan project — not a campaign, a party, or a PAC. Its promises are built to be verified, not trusted: no account, no tracking, and nothing about you kept on a server. citations.title: Cite Oravan
citations.intro: Oravan is built to be a source you can cite and correct: every bill has one permanent address, a dated freshness stamp, and a clear line between the official record and AI-drafted plain language. This page spells out exactly what that promise means — for reporters, librarians, and anyone building on Oravan's data or MCP server — and explains how to report an error.
citations.mcpNoteBody: Building something on top of Oravan's data instead? The MCP server hands the same bill decodes and representative lookups to an AI agent — read-only, keyless, and citation-first.
citations.urlBody: Every bill gets one permanent address in each language, built only from its own bill type, number, and Congress — never from its status. A citation written the day a bill is introduced still resolves after it's signed, fails, or expires; the address is never reused or reassigned.
citations.urlExampleLabel: Example — H.R. 1787, the same bill used in Oravan's own demo material:
citations.asOfBody: Every page states the date of Oravan's last successful nightly sync with Congress.gov — not a live feed, and not the date you happen to load the page. Cite that date, not today's date, as the moment the underlying facts were last checked. It's the same value as the {asOfField} field in every MCP tool response. One exception: the news articles in a bill's "How it's being covered" section don't come from Congress.gov. Coverage is re-checked on its own rotation — the most urgent bills every night, the rest in turn — so the stamp says nothing about how old those articles are. That section prints the date of the newest article it holds — cite that as the coverage's own cutoff, not as a date we last looked; newer coverage may exist that we haven't collected.
citations.sourceBody: Bill status, dates, sponsor, and text come from Congress.gov. Member and district-office data comes from the public-domain unitedstates/congress-legislators project. Both refresh only through Oravan's own nightly sync. The MCP citation envelope states the source in whichever language a query requested — both language versions are shown below, since this page is read by both:
citations.aiBody: Two kinds of text appear on a bill page, and they're never presented the same way. The official record — title, status, sponsor, dates, last action, the Congress.gov link — is copied, not generated. The plain-language layer — the headline, the summary, and the what/who/why/cost sections — is AI-drafted, and no field publishes unless automated gates pass: both languages present, the official record attached, and a schema check on every decode — a decode that comes back missing a required field is discarded rather than stored half-written, and the whole corpus is re-checked before the nightly sync is allowed to publish anything. The Spanish version of that layer is an AI translation of the English decode, produced in the same model call rather than a second reading of the bill, and it clears the same checks: the Spanish is one of those required fields, so a decode without it is never published in English alone. Nonpartisan wording is held two different ways, and we won't blur them: on bill decodes it's a drafting instruction to the model, and on Big Questions it's an enforced vocabulary check that blocks the publish. Wherever AI-drafted content appears — the site, the MCP server, an embed — it carries this label, in the language the request used; both language versions are shown below:
citations.aiCallScript: Call scripts work under a stricter rule still: they're drafted only inside Oravan's own site, and a caller must read and can edit the script before placing a call. Oravan's MCP server never generates one — it hands back a link to the on-site flow instead, so that human-review step can't be bypassed by an agent.
citations.licenseOfficialLabel: The underlying official-record data — U.S. public domain, in both languages:
citations.licenseAiLabel: Oravan's own AI-drafted plain-language content, in both languages:
citations.licenseCoverage: AllSides' outlet-lean ratings, shown in each bill's "Read" section, are used under a separate CC BY-NC license and are excluded from the MCP server and from anything commercial — a website-only feature until that's resolved.
citations.correctionBody: Found something wrong — a mistranslation, a misread status, a plain-language summary that misstates what a bill does? Use the feedback button in the footer of this (or any) page and choose "Something's not working." Name the bill and describe the error — that's the same intake Oravan uses for every other bug report, not a separate correction form.
citations.whenConfirmedTitle: What happens when a correction is confirmed
citations.whenConfirmedBody: A confirmed error is fixed at the source — the same reviewed data both languages' decodes are built from. From there, every surface reading that data updates together on Oravan's next deploy: the bill page, its statically generated share-card image, and the MCP server's tool responses all read the identical file, so there's no separate cache to invalidate. The one thing that doesn't move on its own is the freshness stamp — the site-wide "as of" date and the MCP envelope's {asOfField} field both track Oravan's last successful nightly sync, so they advance at the next scheduled sync run after the fix ships, the same way they do every night. An embeddable widget that carries bill text is still in development, not yet shipped; once it exists, it will read this same corrected data with no separate correction step of its own.
citations.backlogNote: A correction that points to a broader pattern — not a one-off slip — gets tracked for Oravan's ongoing Spanish-language review process rather than patched quietly and forgotten.

terms.title: Terms, in plain language
terms.p1: Oravan is a free, nonpartisan civic tool. It helps you find your members of Congress, understand active bills, and call about them. It is not affiliated with Congress, any government agency, party, or campaign.
terms.p2: Bill summaries, headlines, and call scripts are drafted by AI and are clearly labeled. They can contain mistakes. The official bill text on Congress.gov is always the authority, and you are responsible for reviewing and editing anything before you say it.
terms.p3: Oravan comes with no guarantees. We do our best to keep representative data and bill statuses current, but offices change numbers and bills move daily — verify anything that matters.
terms.p4: What you do with the phone is yours: you place the calls, you choose the words. Be honest, be brief, and be kind to the staffer who answers.
terms.p5: We have no accounts and store nothing about you on our servers; everything personal stays in your browser. The privacy page explains this in full.

embeds.intro: Free, self-serve widgets — no sales call, no account, no server-side data about your visitors. Pick a widget, set a few options, and copy one script tag.

embeds.docsIsolationTitle: An iframe, not a script running on your page
embeds.docsIsolationBody: The widget loads inside a cross-origin iframe, the same browser mechanism that keeps a video embed or a payment form isolated from the page around it. That isn't a policy promise — it's the browser enforcing it. Your page's own scripts, analytics, and tag managers cannot read what a visitor types into the widget or observe anything happening inside it, because they run in a different origin's sandbox.
embeds.docsPrivacyTitle: What the widget collects about your visitors: nothing
embeds.docsPrivacyCookies: Zero cookies. No response from the embed ever sets one.
embeds.docsPrivacyThirdParty: Zero third-party requests. Every asset the widget loads — fonts, styles, data — comes from Oravan's own origin. Nothing calls out to an ad network, an analytics vendor, or any other third party.
embeds.docsPrivacyZip: ZIP code only. The representative-lookup widget never asks for a street address inside the iframe; a visitor who needs the more precise, split-district lookup is linked out to the main Oravan site for that step.
embeds.docsPrivacyNoData: No visitor data reaches Oravan beyond an ordinary page load. A ZIP code a visitor enters is used once, in memory, to answer that one lookup, and is never logged or stored.
embeds.docsPrivacyTested: These aren't claims made only in this copy — they're enforced by automated tests in Oravan's own public repository, on every change, before it ships.
embeds.docsThemingBody: Theming works the same on all widgets and is limited to a closed set of CSS custom properties, each validated on Oravan's server before it can reach a style: an accent color, an optional background/text color pair (accepted only when it meets the WCAG AA contrast bar of 4.5:1), a color mode (light, dark, or match the visitor's system), a corner-radius style (sharp, soft, or round), and a font (system, serif, humanist, or geometric — all system font stacks; the widget never loads webfonts). There's no way to inject arbitrary CSS or JavaScript into the widget — that's a deliberate security boundary, not a missing feature.
embeds.docsAttributionBody: Every widget shows a small "Powered by Oravan" link, pointing back to the canonical page on oravan.org. The brandless option removes the Oravan name from the widget chrome (its accessible titles and fallback labels) but keeps that attribution link — it's how the free tier stays free. Removing attribution itself (data-attribution="none") is reserved for licensed partners: there's no technical lock yet, so we say it plainly — if you want it, write us for a license. The AI-content label is never removable, on any tier.
embeds.docsLoaderBody: The script tag your snippet includes is a single, dependency-free file under 5KB. All it does is create the iframe, size it to fit its content, and relay that size back — nothing is read from your page, and nothing is sent anywhere except the one request that loads the widget itself.
embeds.whiteLabelNote: Removes the Oravan name from widget titles and fallback labels. The "Powered by Oravan" link stays on — removing it is available to licensed partners only; see the attribution note below.
embeds.docsFeedBody: A free, keyless JSON and RSS feed of bills that cleared Oravan's "act now" urgency bar in the last 7 days — the same list the homepage shows. No token, no signup: point a newsletter tool or an RSS reader straight at it. Every AI-generated item carries the AI-content label, and the feed's own attribution line is permanent at every use.
embeds.docsTosBody: Institutional and commercial use of these widgets — Free, Pro, Nonprofit, and Network plans alike — is governed by a separate Terms of Service from the one that covers Oravan's free citizen site.
embeds.docsTosLinkText: Read the embeds Terms of Service
embeds.docsManageBody: Subscribers on a paid plan can update their payment method, download invoices, and cancel at any time through Stripe's secure billing portal — sign in there with the email you used at checkout. Oravan itself holds no account and no payment details.

embedsTerms.title: Embeds Terms of Service
embedsTerms.citizenTermsLinkText: Looking for the citizen-site Terms instead?
embedsTerms.intro: These Terms of Service govern institutional and commercial use of Oravan Embeds — the widget products described at /embeds, at every tier (Free, Pro, Nonprofit, and Network). They are separate from, and do not replace, the Terms that govern Oravan's free citizen product.
embedsTerms.governingLanguageNotice: This document is authored in, and controls in, English. Any Spanish-language version of this page is provided only as a courtesy translation; in the event of any conflict or ambiguity between the two, the English text governs.
embedsTerms.scopeBody: These terms apply to any organization ("Tenant") that embeds an Oravan widget under a Free, Pro, Nonprofit, or Network plan, or that accepts these terms through Stripe Checkout. They do not apply to an individual visitor of a Tenant's site, and they do not apply to Oravan's own citizen-facing site, which is governed by a separate, simpler Terms page.
embedsTerms.nonpartisanBody: Oravan is nonpartisan by construction. A Tenant may not represent an Oravan widget as endorsing, opposing, or taking a position on any candidate, party, or ballot measure; may not frame a widget with advocacy chrome — calls-to-action, imagery, or surrounding copy — that implies Oravan holds or shares the Tenant's stance on any issue; and may not use a widget to capture, solicit, or profile a visitor's political position, party affiliation, or voting intent. Content stays nonpartisan in both English and Spanish, at every tier, with no exceptions.
embedsTerms.attributionBody: Free-tier widgets display a "Powered by Oravan" attribution link at all times; it may not be hidden, obscured, or styled to be illegible. Paid tiers may remove the Oravan name from widget chrome ("brandless") but the attribution link itself stays on unless Oravan has granted attribution removal in writing to a licensed partner. The AI-content disclosure label is never removable, hideable, or overridable at any tier — it is a safety and honesty label, not a branding element.
embedsTerms.prohibitedItem1: inject custom CSS or JavaScript into a widget, or attempt to break the iframe's isolation from the host page;
embedsTerms.prohibitedItem2: scrape, bulk-download, or programmatically re-request widget or feed data beyond normal rate limits, or use that data to build a competing lookup or bill-decode product;
embedsTerms.prohibitedItem3: sublicense, resell, or share a capability token with any organization other than the Tenant itself, absent a written Network-tier agreement naming that organization;
embedsTerms.prohibitedItem4: misrepresent the source, ownership, or neutrality of embedded content, or alter AI-generated text without disclosing the alteration.
embedsTerms.tokenBody: A Tenant is responsible for keeping its capability token confidential and for any use of the widget that token authorizes. The domain allowlist Oravan checks against a widget's Referer/Origin is a best-effort convenience, not a security guarantee — a determined actor can strip or spoof that header. Oravan may rotate or revoke a Tenant's token at any time on suspicion of compromise, abuse, or a violation of these terms, with notice to the Tenant's billing email where practical. A Tenant may request rotation at any time by contacting Oravan.
embedsTerms.licensingBody: No embed, at any tier, includes outlet political-lean ratings or any other content from Oravan's "Read" coverage section. That data is licensed to Oravan on a non-commercial basis and is never distributed through any paid or embeddable surface.
embedsTerms.billingBody: Paid plans are billed and processed through Stripe; Oravan does not separately store payment details. Plans are self-serve, cancel-anytime, and monthly or annual as selected at checkout, except Network-tier agreements, which are billed as separately negotiated.
embedsTerms.warrantyBody: Oravan provides the embeds product on a best-effort basis, with no warranty of uptime, accuracy, or fitness for a particular purpose. Bill and representative data is refreshed nightly and can be briefly delayed or incorrect; AI-generated content can contain mistakes and is never a substitute for the official bill text linked from every response.

partners.title: Partners
partners.intro: Oravan's widgets are built to live inside other people's pages — newsroom articles, library guides, an organization's action center. Everything on this page is free to use today; here's what each kind of partner gets, and where the licensed tier begins.
partners.newsroomsBody: Drop a representative lookup or a plain-language bill card into any article — two script tags, no account, no tracking of your readers, ever. Spanish ships as a peer surface, not an afterthought: every interface string is written in both languages, a bill's plain-language layer is AI-translated from the English decode, and neither language publishes without the other — so an es-first outlet embeds an es-first widget, complete on the day it goes live. Theme it to your section colors, or use brandless chrome so the widget reads as part of your page.
partners.librariesBody: Oravan is safe to put in front of every patron: strictly nonpartisan by construction, no accounts, nothing stored server-side, and plain language that never publishes without passing automated checks against the official record. Link it from a resource guide or embed the lookup on your programs page — it works the same on a library terminal as on a phone.
partners.orgsBody: Nonprofits, unions, and civic groups use the same free widgets as everyone else — themed, in either language, with attribution. A licensed tier for organizations that need attribution-free white-label embeds is coming; the capability exists today and is documented on the embeds page.
partners.licensingBody: If your organization wants white-label embeds, attribution removal, or a data partnership, email hello@oravan.org — it reaches a real person directly. Pricing isn't published yet. You can also use the feedback link at the bottom of any page and choose “Partnership or licensing” if you'd rather not email.

mcp.title: Oravan's MCP server
mcp.intro: Oravan also speaks MCP (the Model Context Protocol) — the same federal bill decodes and representative lookups the website shows, callable directly by an AI assistant. It's free, read-only, and keyless: no account, no API key, and every response states exactly where its facts came from.
mcp.endpointBody: Any MCP client that supports Streamable HTTP can connect at the address below — the same live server described on this page, not a preview or a sandbox.
mcp.connectBody: In Claude Desktop, claude.ai's custom connectors, or any other client that reads a JSON config, add an entry pointing at the endpoint above. Most Streamable-HTTP-aware clients accept a shape close to this:
mcp.toolsIntro: Every tool is read-only and closed-world — none of them writes anything, and none reaches outside Oravan's own nightly-synced data. The name, title, and description below are quoted exactly as the live server sends them to a calling agent.
mcp.toolsLangNote: Tool names and descriptions are protocol metadata a calling AI model reads to decide how to use a tool, not prose written for a person — so, like every MCP server, Oravan defines them in English only. Everything a tool call actually hands back to a conversation is fully bilingual: the citation envelope below, every error message, and any AI-drafted content all honor the language a query requests.
mcp.privacyNoAccounts: No accounts and no API key — anyone can call it, the same way anyone can load the website.
mcp.privacyRateLimit: Anonymous use is rate-limited (60 calls a minute, 1,000 a day) by a short-lived, hashed counter — never a stored IP address, and never linked to what was asked.
mcp.privacyNoLogging: Nothing here is logged in a way that could connect a caller to a bill, a representative, or a political position.
mcp.envelopeBody: Every tool response nests a meta object with five fields: as_of (the data's freshness date), source, canonical_url (a stable link back to the page an agent's answer came from), ai_label (present only when the response includes AI-drafted content), and license. The source and AI-label text are shown below in both languages, matching what an English- or Spanish-locale query actually receives — the same strings Oravan's citability page quotes.
mcp.licenseOfficialLabel: Official-record fields — status, dates, sponsor, bill text:
mcp.licenseAiLabel: AI-drafted plain-language fields — headline, tl;dr, what/who/why/cost:
mcp.freshnessBody: Oravan's data refreshes on a nightly sync with Congress.gov, not a live feed. Every tool response's {asOfField} field states the date of the last successful sync — cite that date, not the moment a query ran, as when the underlying facts were last checked.

moments.emptyTitle: No live Big Questions right now
moments.emptyBody: A Big Question opens only when a real, callable bill or Senate nomination meets the published criteria below — not because a story is loud. Browse everything moving through Congress instead.

moments.settledBanner: This question is settled — here's what happened. This page stays as the record and won't reopen.
moments.staleBanner: This Big Question's scheduled review ({date}) passed without renewal — it may not reflect where things stand right now.
moments.vehiclesLede: The bills this question actually runs through. Each opens the full plain-language decode and the call flow — support and oppose scripts are equally one tap away.
moments.vehiclesLedeNominations: The Senate nominations this question actually runs through. Each opens the Senate's own record — and, where that record shows a decision the Senate can still make, the call flow, with support and oppose scripts equally one tap away.
moments.vehiclesLedeMixed: The bills and Senate nominations this question actually runs through. Each opens the record — and, where that record still has a call to make, the call flow, with support and oppose scripts equally one tap away.
moments.vehiclesAiNote: Plain-language text on these cards — the decoded headline, where there is one, and the summary of what a yes and a no vote do — is AI-drafted and labeled. Nothing publishes until it passes automated checks, and every page carries a one-tap way to flag an error.
moments.bothNote: No side is pre-selected. Every link above opens the same call flow, with support and oppose scripts equally available.
moments.bothNoteSomeNoCall: No side is pre-selected. Where a record still has a call to make, the same call flow opens, with support and oppose scripts equally available.
moments.whyCriteria: A Big Question opens only when a live, callable bill or Senate nomination meets published criteria: a government scheduling or floor-action signal, or press coverage from outlets across the spectrum, within the last 45 days.

signalType.press: Covered by outlets across the spectrum

moments.howMadeBody: A Big Question opens only when something real before Congress meets every rule below — checked by an automated gate, then reviewed by a person before it publishes.
moments.howMadeRule1: Something still moving: at least one tracked bill or Senate nomination that has not reached its end. The question has to still be one a call can affect.
moments.howMadeRule2: A recent signal: in the last 45 days it appeared on a government schedule or in a chamber's own floor proceedings (a floor vote, a motion or cloture filing on the floor, the week's bill list, Congress.gov's most-viewed, the Senate Executive Calendar), or in press coverage from at least two outlets of differing leanings.
moments.howMadeRule3: A callable action: the page and the call script already work — every corpus bill qualifies by construction, and a nomination qualifies only when the Senate's record carries the description sentence its script is written from. The gate rejects one that doesn't.
moments.howMadeRule4: A neutral name: a description of the disagreement either side would recognize as fair, never one side's own label for it.
moments.lifecycleLive: This Big Question retires when the question is settled — every bill signed, vetoed, or dead, and every nomination confirmed, returned, or withdrawn. Settled Big Questions stay readable, marked resolved; they never reopen.
moments.aiNote: Every Big Question's name and summary are AI-drafted from the public record and labeled. Nothing publishes until it passes automated checks — both languages, the record attached, no advocacy language.

reason.newActions: {count, plural, one {# new action was recorded} other {# new actions were recorded}} since the last version
reason.statusMoved: a bill on this question moved to a different stage
reason.reanchor: {days, plural, one {# day had passed} other {# days had passed}} since the last version

updates.timelineLede: Everything the record shows on this question's bills, newest day first — a Senate nomination's own record lives on its page. Up to {cap} a day are listed here, and the days nothing was recorded are shown as they were.
updates.timelineAiChip: The one-line decodes below are AI-written from the official action text.
updates.checkGapNote: we have not been able to check for new activity since {date}

updates.privacyNote: Nobody is watching you read this — no account, no tracking, no feed tuned to you, which is why the same page can be shared across the spectrum.

nominations.metaDescription: A presidential nomination pending before the U.S. Senate — the Senate's own record of it, and the call that goes with it.
nominations.metaDescriptionNoCall: A presidential nomination before the U.S. Senate — the Senate's own record of it. This one carries no call script.
nominations.noDecodeNote: Oravan does not rewrite nominations. This is the Senate's own record, word for word.
nominations.recordLede: Congress.gov's own entry for this nomination. The Senate's action text below is reproduced word for word; the labels, the date formatting and the notes around it are Oravan's.

closed.confirmed: The Senate voted to confirm this nomination. A confirmed nomination is finished — there is no call left to make on it.
closed.returned: The Senate returned this nomination to the President without confirming it. There is no call left to make on it.
closed.withdrawn: The President withdrew this nomination. There is no call left to make on it.

nominations.noScriptBody: The Senate's entry for this nomination carries no description — nothing that says who it is for or what post it fills. That sentence is the only thing a call script here is ever built from, so Oravan offers none rather than inventing words about a record that says nothing. The nomination is still before the Senate, and everything the Senate has published about it is on this page, in full.

status.unclassified: Stage not stated in the record

langNote.dismiss: No volver a mostrar este aviso
